rv.q: It’s a lovely Chicago play, brought thrillingly back to Broadway life.
Cheadle, Young, and Ha deliver effortless portrayals.
Add to that Edebiri, who, while not giving the career-defining performance Parker did, is nonetheless worth seeing.
She wobbles badly under that weight.
It gets where it needs to go; what it lacks, at least for now, is elegance.

Still, the father-daughter pair does, at least, perform charmingly together. Cheadle and Edebiri are both down-to-earth and unshowy in their clear affection for each other, and they’re warmly believable as parent and child. Cheadle is laid back to the point of liquidity; he’s the only star I’ve ever...
As it is, the show comes off lumpy and soft, with the inelegancies of the text left exposed and its sharper points insufficiently filed.
It all adds up to one exceptional piece of theater.
Broadway just got smarter and deeper thanks to the return of David Auburn’s Proof, a complex, curvy, and thoroughly compelling play motored by a math-related mystery.
Edebiri and Cheadle are about to make something special of their Broadway debuts.
Her mix of physical comedy, well-timed quips, and heartbreaking reveals must be seen to be believed.
“Proof” remains the same appealing play – part family drama, part comedy, part mystery – that it was a quarter century ago
Both sides of that equation are why Thomas Kail’s current Broadway revival at the Booth Theatre is generally effective, but rarely as emotionally charged as it should be.
There’s a big hole in the middle of this “Proof.”
But Kail’s spiritless revival fails to tap into the play’s specific collision of expansive ideas and fervid emotion.

Indeed, for all its prior accolades, “Proof” rarely rises above being a compelling character study, without much implication of any larger questions outside those four Chicago walls. However, with such fine acting on display, there’s more than enough to warrant a visit (return to otherwise) and the ...
And yet director Thomas Kail’s production feels more dutiful than deep, an oddly bloodless exercise in melodrama that keeps its passions bundled up as if girding for a frigid Chicago winter.
Broadway’s first revival of Proof brings the star wattage, but can’t find the current running through David Auburn’s play.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.
